# What holds up on HYPE? Strategies, patterns and price levels

Over two years of daily HYPE candles, no tested rule beat holding the coin, and trend rules only reduced the worst decline. No short-term pattern tested passed its controls, and past price levels held no more often than arbitrary lines nearby. Rules that won on shorter windows won in one market direction or one week.

Version: 1.0.0
Date: 2026-11-27
Author: Oraclebot Research
Status: Working paper. Historical backtests and descriptive statistics; not peer reviewed, not prospectively validated. Nothing was traded.

[Download the paper as PDF](https://oraclebot.io/papers/hype-strategies-patterns-levels.pdf)

## Abstract

We ask three questions about HYPE, the Hyperliquid token: which trading rules performed best, which price patterns exist, and where support and resistance lie. We use one gap-free week of Binance spot minute bars (10,080 bars; 1,707 strategy templates give 491,712 test rows), two years of Hyperliquid daily bars (722) and 208 days of hourly bars (4,999). Every rule pays modelled costs, and all are long or flat except one synthetic long/short reference model. Over two years, holding returned +389% with a 68% worst decline, and none of 30 distinct rules beat it; a 20/50-day moving-average crossover kept +173% with a 40% worst decline. On hourly bars, trend rules beat holding only because they stood aside during a 28.6% fall, and no rule made money in both the rising and the falling part. Within one week, ATR-sized trend following (stops set by average true range) on 5- and 10-minute bars returned +14% to +16% at 10 basis points (bps) per fill and passed a validation-and-test screen at 10 and 60 bps, but a separate 31-day run found the same family losing. The ZEC (Zcash) two-bar reversal, candle shapes and leading correlations fail on HYPE, and the cycle tests were inconclusive. Swing levels held 10% to 48% of the time, no better than placebo lines. We publish the level map as reference prices, not as signals.

## 1. Three questions, short answers

**Which strategies performed best?** The answer changes with the bar size and with whether the market was rising or falling. No rule won at every bar size. Over two years nothing beat holding.

| Horizon | Leading rule | Result | How far to trust it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Daily, two years | Buy and hold | +389%, with a 68% worst decline | No tested rule beat it. A 20/50-day moving-average crossover kept +173% with a 40% worst decline. |
| Hourly, 208 days | Bollinger breakout (20 bars, 2 deviations) | +107% against +59% for holding at 6 bps, with a 17% worst decline against 42% | It made all of it in the rising part and lost 1.5% in the falling part. At 25 bps it made +49% and trailed holding. |
| 5 and 10 minutes, one week | ATR-sized trend following | +14% to +16% in a week where holding made +0.3% to +0.5% | Positive in validation and in the final test, at 10 and at 60 bps per fill. The screen uses the final test, so this is exploratory. One week only, and a separate 31-day run found the family losing. |
| 1 hour, one week | Average of MACD, PPO and RSI | +4.6% | Positive in validation and in the final test at every fee level. Small. |
| Falling market, hourly | Oversold bounce (RSI under 30 plus a lower-band touch) | +26.7% while holding lost 28.6% | It lost 1.2% in the rising part before that. Its result depended on the market's direction. |
| 1 minute | Nothing | 68 of 1,707 rules made money at the lowest fee, 19 at the highest | None passed the validation-and-test screen. |

Costs are charged per fill in basis points (bps; one basis point is 0.01%), as section 3 describes. "Leading" is not one measure: the daily and hourly rows name the highest total return, the falling-market row a rule that made money in the falling part, and the one-week rows the best rules that passed the strict screen in section 3. Rules that failed that screen returned more over the week at 10 bps, up to about +19%. The one-week rows come from the 1,707-template catalogue. A separate synthetic long/short model in section 4.1 returned more over the week at 10 bps in its best screened settings (+17.9% on 10-minute bars, +28.6% on 1-hour bars). It is kept apart because it goes short and pays a flat carry, not real funding.

**Which patterns exist?** HYPE falls far and often: seven declines of 25% or more in two years. It has no day-to-day memory. It moves with Bitcoin and moves further. A quarter of its volume trades between 13:00 and 16:59 UTC. Weekday effects, hour-of-day direction, the ZEC two-bar reversal (section 5.3), candle shapes and leading correlations did not survive their controls, and the cycle tests were inconclusive.

**Where are support and resistance?** Section 6 gives the map. At the time of the study the Hyperliquid price was $65.40. The nearest zones above were $65.43–66.14, $67.76–68.34 and $68.62–70.25; the nearest below were $64.50–65.10, $62.42–63.35, a single hourly swing low at $61.64, and $59.70–60.55. Past returns to such levels broke them more often than they held, and they held no more often than arbitrary lines nearby.

## 2. Data

| Study | Market | Span | Bars |
|---|---|---|---:|
| One week of minute bars | Binance spot HYPE/USDT | 2026-11-20 08:49 to 2026-11-27 08:49 UTC | 10,080 one-minute bars, none missing |
| Two years of daily bars | Hyperliquid HYPE perpetual | 2024-12-05 to 2026-11-26 | 722 |
| 208 days of hourly bars | Hyperliquid HYPE perpetual | 2026-05-03 to 2026-11-27 | 4,999 |
| Reference coins | Hyperliquid BTC, ETH and SOL perpetuals, daily | 2023-11-14 to 2026-11-26 | 1,109 each |

The data were frozen on 2026-11-27 between 08:49 and 08:53 UTC. HYPE traded near $65.60 on Binance spot, and the last completed Hyperliquid hour closed at $65.40.

Choosing the source was itself a finding. We checked three venues that carry HYPE candles, and each has a limit that decides what it can be used for.

- **Coinbase HYPE/USD has gaps in its minute candles.** A separate Coinbase run found that the longest gap-free minute run in 31 days was 46 hours. A minute study built on it would be a study of two days. We did not use it.
- **Binance HYPE/USDT is gap-free but short.** Its minute history is confirmed here from 2026-10-27; a first daily candle dated 2026-09-24 was seen at fetch time and not archived. That is enough for a week or a month of minute bars and too short for a two-year history.
- **Hyperliquid has the long history, as perpetual prices.** HYPE has traded there since late 2024. Its candle endpoint returned only the latest 5,000 hourly bars, so the hourly history reaches back 208 days.

USDT is not USD, and a perpetual is not spot. The data table above names the market for each study. Hyperliquid perpetual prices can differ slightly from Binance spot: the week's high was $69.70 on Hyperliquid and $69.80 on Binance.

## 3. Method

The tests repeat, for HYPE, a set of studies first run on ZEC (Zcash), known as the ZEC suite.

**Long or flat.** Every rule either holds HYPE or holds cash, with one exception: the synthetic long/short breakout-stop model in section 4.1. No short side with real funding was tested. This matters for reading the results: in a market that rose 389%, any rule that stays invested much of the time collects part of the rise.

**Fills and costs.** A signal on a closed bar fills at the next bar's open. Costs are charged on every fill, in basis points (bps; one basis point is 0.01%). The week of minute bars is tested at 10, 15, 25 and 60 bps per fill, each with a further 2 bps execution allowance. The daily and hourly tests charge a 6 bps fee and 2 bps slippage, and are repeated at 25 bps. Reference accounts hold 10,000 units of the quote currency. There is no model of order-book depth.

**Out-of-sample splits.** The week is cut in time order into a training part (60%), a validation part (20%) and a final-test part (20%). One selection rule was frozen before the final test was read: take the rule with the best validation return among those with at least ten validation exits, and never re-rank on the final test. The daily and hourly histories are cut into a first 70% and a last 30%, and every registered strategy runs with its default parameters. Each part is run on its own, so the two parts need not compound exactly to the whole.

**The strict screen.** For the week we also report every rule that had at least ten validation exits and a positive return in validation, in the final test and over the whole week, at both 10 and 60 bps. Because this screen also uses the final test, it is exploratory and not out-of-sample evidence; the frozen selection rule above is the only choice made before the final test.

**Strategy catalogue.** The week tests 1,707 strategy templates, each with six filter or control variants, on four bar sizes at four fee levels and over three windows (whole week, validation and final test), plus cash and holding benchmarks: 491,712 rows, of which 441,888 completed. It also runs 7,920 rows of breakout-stop, ladder-grid and dollar-cost-averaging reference models. The long histories run the 34 strategies registered in the project's backtester (the simulation code in the repository linked in section 10), of which 30 are distinct (the registry also lists holding itself and three duplicate MACD entries).

**Price levels.** A swing level is a high or low that was the extreme of 5 days on each side (daily) or 24 hours on each side (hourly). Swings are grouped so that no group is wider than 3% (daily) or 1.2% (hourly). A level is tested only after the bar that confirms it, and only while it is unbroken. Section 6 describes the test and its placebo.

**Corrections for many tests.** Where one question is asked many times, we say how many and what threshold that implies. Seven weekdays need a t-statistic near 2.7 and 24 hours need one above 3 before a single row counts as more than chance.

## 4. Strategy results

### 4.1 One week of minute bars

The week ended where it began: $65.63 to $65.60, between $55.80 and $69.80. The training part fell 4.9%, the validation part fell 1.5% and the final-test part rose 6.8%.

Share of the 1,707 unfiltered rules that made money over the whole week:

| Bar size | At 10 bps per fill | At 60 bps per fill | Holding, 10 bps |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 minute | 4.0% | 1.1% | −0.2% |
| 5 minutes | 44.1% | 4.9% | +0.3% |
| 10 minutes | 65.4% | 10.0% | +0.5% |
| 1 hour (1,027 completed) | 66.4% | 38.7% | +0.6% |

Costs decide the one-minute result. A rule that trades every few minutes pays the fee hundreds of times in a week, and almost none of them earn it back.

Twelve distinct 5-minute rules pass the strict screen (nine ATR-sized, two GARCH volatility-target, one volatility-target), with three 10-minute rules and three 1-hour rules. No 1-minute rule passes. ATR is the average true range, a measure of how far price moves per bar; an ATR-sized rule follows the trend, risks a fixed share of the account per trade and sets its stop a multiple of ATR away.

| Bars | Rule | Whole week, 10 bps | Whole week, 60 bps | Validation / test, 60 bps | Worst decline | Exits |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 5m | ATR-sized: ATR 45, risk 1%, stop 2 ATR, trend 200 | +16.3% | +4.1% | +2.6% / +3.5% | −6.4% | 76 |
| 5m | ATR-sized: ATR 30, risk 1%, stop 1.5 ATR, trend 200 | +16.5% | +4.0% | +3.6% / +3.5% | −7.4% | 40 |
| 10m | ATR-sized: ATR 30, risk 1%, stop 2 ATR, trend 100 | +14.3% | +4.1% | +1.2% / +0.7% | −4.6% | 98 |
| 1h | Average of MACD 12/26/9, PPO 12/26/9 and RSI 14 (30 → 50) | +4.6% | +0.5% | +1.3% / +0.6% | −5.7% | 40 |

What the frozen selection rule picked, and what the pick did on the final test at each fee level:

| Bars | Picked on validation | Validation, 10 bps | Final test at 10 / 15 / 25 / 60 bps | Test exits |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| 1m | Moving-average ribbon with a slope filter (a volatility-target rule at 60 bps) | +5.0% | −1.7% / −3.1% / −5.8% / −0.5% | 325 to 445 |
| 5m | ATR-sized, ATR 30 (a momentum and swing gate at 25 bps) | +4.8% | +6.6% / +6.3% / +0.3% / +3.5% | 3 (30 at 25 bps) |
| 10m | MACD and on-balance-volume gate | +6.7% | +0.6% / −0.1% / −1.5% / −6.2% | 17 |
| 1h | Average of MACD, PPO and RSI | +2.6% | +1.9% / +1.8% / +1.5% / +0.6% | 14 |

The 5-minute pick returned +6.6% in the final test on three exits, while holding returned +6.8%. So the test shows that the rule did not lose in a rally. It does not show that the rule beats holding in one. Under 3.2% of rules beat holding in the final test at any bar size. The 1-minute and 10-minute picks did not hold up. The 1-hour pick stayed positive at every fee level.

The table gives the median whole-week return of single-rule strategies on 5-minute bars at 10 bps, grouped by rule family. About one in eight of these strategies also carries a gate or a switch, and each family spans several parameter settings:

| Best families | Median | Worst families | Median |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| ATR-sized trend | +9.9% | PPO | −15.5% |
| Moving-average regime | +9.0% | Dual momentum | −13.3% |
| EMA crossover | +8.4% | MACD | −8.7% |
| Keltner breakout | +8.1% | Z-score reversion | −8.0% |
| Ichimoku | +6.9% | Bollinger reversion, stochastic | −7.3% |

On 5-minute bars this week, slow trend filters with wide stops made money, and fast oscillators and reversion rules lost. That did not hold on 1-minute bars. There the ATR-sized family's median was −31.5%, and no family had a positive median except dollar-cost averaging.

Three reference models from the ZEC suite, at 10 bps:

- **Breakout stops, synthetic 1× long and short.** On 1-minute bars none of 150 runs made money. On 5-minute bars 3% did. On 1-hour bars 60% did, and 13 of 50 settings were positive in validation and in the final test even on the least favourable assumption about the order of prices inside a bar. The best of those, length 2 with 1.25 ATR, made +28.6% over the week. On 10-minute bars six settings passed the same screen; length 4 with 1.25 ATR made +17.9%. This is the only model here that goes short, and it is synthetic: it pays a flat carry, not real funding.
- **Ladder grid.** All eight reference grids made money on 5-minute and 1-hour bars (median +2.2% and +2.7%, best +4.2%). The week's range suited a grid.
- **Dollar-cost averaging with safety orders.** Ten of twelve were positive on 5-minute bars and all twelve on 1-hour bars (median +0.3% and +0.6%, best +4.8%).

### 4.2 Two years of daily bars

Hyperliquid perpetual candles, 2024-12-05 to 2026-11-26. Long or cash, 6 bps fee plus 2 bps slippage. The first 70% ends on 2026-04-23. The table shows the six highest total returns and holding; the long-history evidence in section 10 has every row.

| Strategy | Total return | Sharpe | Worst decline | Trades | First 70% | Last 30% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Buy and hold | +389.4% | 1.29 | −68.0% | 1 | +224.7% | +51.0% |
| Dollar-cost averaging, 10 buys 7 days apart | +194.5% | 1.04 | −64.2% | 30 | +95.4% | +19.1% |
| Moving-average crossover 20/50 | +172.7% | 1.09 | −39.7% | 6 | +107.8% | +31.5% |
| Moving-average ribbon 5×10 | +138.4% | 1.03 | −42.2% | 209 | +71.6% | +39.2% |
| Time-series momentum, 60 days | +124.6% | 0.94 | −58.3% | 16 | +77.9% | +26.4% |
| VWAP reversion 20 / 2% | +96.9% | 0.84 | −46.9% | 41 | +51.0% | +30.5% |
| Volatility target 60% | +89.7% | 0.93 | −44.3% | 180 | +54.5% | +22.9% |

Dollar-cost averaging is holding with a delayed start: it is fully invested after about ten weeks and keeps almost all of the worst decline. Fourteen of the 27 strategies with a split result made money in both parts; three could not be run on the split. None beat holding in either part, and the 50/200 EMA crossover matched it in the last 30%. Reversion rules made money here too: Z-score +83.5% and stochastic +76.4%, against +29.4% for the Bollinger breakout. That is the long-or-flat effect described in section 3, not evidence for reversion.

At 25 bps the crossover still returned +166.6% and the ribbon +125.7%. The case for the crossover is risk, not return: it gave up 56% of the gain, and its worst decline was 42% smaller.

### 4.3 208 days of hourly bars

2026-05-03 to 2026-11-27. The first 70% (to 2026-09-25) rose 122%. The last 30% fell 28.6%. The table shows the four rules that beat holding, holding itself, and the two bounce rules.

| Strategy | Total return | Sharpe | Worst decline | Trades | First 70% | Last 30% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Bollinger breakout 20 / 2 | +106.8% | 2.78 | −17.0% | 86 | +110.0% | −1.5% |
| EMA crossover 50/200 | +87.9% | 2.07 | −22.7% | 10 | +91.9% | −1.3% |
| 200-bar average regime | +83.2% | 2.02 | −25.8% | 78 | +104.2% | −10.3% |
| ADX trend 14 / 25 | +70.8% | 2.22 | −22.6% | 82 | +103.3% | −16.0% |
| Buy and hold | +58.8% | 1.37 | −42.1% | 1 | +122.4% | −28.6% |
| Oversold bounce (RSI < 30 and lower-band touch) | +25.2% | 2.41 | −8.8% | 60 | −1.2% | +26.7% |
| RSI 14 (30 → 50) | +9.1% | 0.60 | −21.9% | 35 | −3.2% | +12.7% |

No strategy made money in both parts. The trend rules beat holding because they stood aside for most of the fall. The bounce rules made money only in the fall. At 25 bps only the EMA crossover (+80.9%) still beat holding (+58.2%), and the oversold bounce fell to −0.3% overall.

This is the paper's clearest example of a ranking that depends on the window. On hourly bars the best rule depends on which part of the history is used to judge it. At the September split holding had the highest return and the trend rules the highest return for the risk taken. In the fall that followed, the trend rules lost money, though less than holding did, and the bounce rules that had looked worst made money.

### 4.4 What borrowing costs

A 1× perpetual long, run under the Jupiter-style hourly borrow fee built into the project's backtester (Jupiter is a Solana perpetuals exchange), kept +143.4% of the +389.4%. It paid $15,084 in borrow fees on a $10,000 account and was liquidated once in the model. This is a stress case for a borrow fee of that kind. It is not Hyperliquid's funding, which was not modelled. The run allowed short positions, but no registered strategy emits one at its default settings, so it tests the borrow fee and nothing else.

## 5. Patterns

### 5.1 Where price stood

| Measure | Value |
|---|---:|
| Last hourly close | $65.40 |
| Last completed daily close | $62.25 |
| All-time high in this history | $98.00 on 2026-09-23 |
| Daily close against that high | −36.5% |
| Lowest low in this history | $9.31 on 2025-04-07 |
| Annualized volatility, two years | 102% |
| Annualized volatility, last 30 days | 83% |
| Average true range, 14 days | 9.7% of price |
| 20-day average close | $67.72 |
| 50-day average close | $76.13 |
| 100-day average close | $80.69 |
| 200-day average close | $70.40 |

The daily close was below all four averages.

### 5.2 What the data supports

**Large, frequent declines.** Seven declines of 25% or more since December 2024. The PDF edition charts them as Figure 1.

| Peak | Trough | Depth | Days down | New high |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| $35.35 on 2024-12-21 | $9.31 on 2025-04-07 | −73.7% | 107 | 2025-05-23 |
| $45.84 on 2025-06-16 | $30.25 on 2025-06-21 | −34.0% | 5 | 2025-07-11 |
| $49.89 on 2025-07-14 | $35.48 on 2025-08-02 | −28.9% | 19 | 2025-08-27 |
| $59.47 on 2025-09-18 | $20.46 on 2026-01-21 | −65.6% | 125 | 2026-05-21 |
| $75.83 on 2026-06-01 | $52.61 on 2026-06-10 | −30.6% | 9 | 2026-06-16 |
| $77.00 on 2026-06-16 | $51.08 on 2026-08-02 | −33.7% | 47 | 2026-08-21 |
| $98.00 on 2026-09-23 | $55.74 on 2026-11-21 | −43.1% | 59 | not yet |

The depths run from peak price to trough price, so they are not the same measure as the worst decline in the backtests of section 4. A decline is counted as finished only when price makes a new high. The six finished ones are too few to say how the present one ends.

**No day-to-day memory.** The correlation between one day's return and the next is +0.009, and it stays within ±0.03 out to five days. Hourly returns are similar: −0.034 at one hour. Volatility clusters mildly: the correlation between the sizes of consecutive daily moves is +0.116.

**Bitcoin beta above one.** Daily correlation with BTC is 0.54 and beta is 1.26 over two years: when Bitcoin moved 1%, HYPE moved 1.26% on average. With ETH the figures are 0.56 and 0.83, with SOL 0.56 and 0.74. Over the last 90 days the BTC figures are 0.59 and 1.04. Within the week of minute bars the same-minute correlation with BTC was 0.73. Moving together is not a signal: section 5.3 shows that neither BTC nor ZEC led HYPE within the week. ETH and SOL were not tested for a lead.

**A US-hours volume peak.** 13:00–16:59 UTC carries 26.4% of hourly volume. Average absolute hourly moves peak at 0.82–0.83% at 14:00 and 15:00 UTC and bottom at 0.49–0.50% at 06:00 and 09:00 UTC. This is a fact about when HYPE moves, not about which way.

**Swings of 1% a few hours apart (a description, not a test).** In the week of minute bars, 1% peaks came a median 145 minutes apart and dips 158 minutes apart. The spacing was more even than 95% of shuffled paths in 5 of 24 comparisons, uncorrected. The formal cycle tests in section 5.3 found no clock to trade on.

### 5.3 What the data does not support

**Weekday effects.** Wednesday averaged +1.26% (t = 2.18, 103 days), Tuesday −0.31% and Thursday −0.42%. Seven tests need a t-statistic near 2.7. None reaches it.

**Hour-of-day direction.** 01:00 UTC averaged −0.13% (t = −2.17). Twenty-four tests need a t-statistic above 3. None reaches it.

**Buying big down days.**

| Condition | Days | Next-day average | Standard error | Next day up |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| All days | 720 | +0.35% | 0.20% | 51% |
| After any up day | 367 | +0.17% | 0.28% | 49% |
| After any down day | 353 | +0.54% | 0.29% | 53% |
| After a gain of 5% or more | 119 | +1.06% | 0.59% | 53% |
| After a loss of 5% or more | 89 | +0.81% | 0.63% | 55% |
| After a gain of 10% or more | 35 | +1.86% | 1.12% | 54% |
| After a loss of 10% or more | 18 | +2.30% | 1.26% | 61% |

Days after a 10% loss and days after a 10% gain were both followed by above-average returns. Neither case separates from the other, and each is within two standard errors of the average day.

**The ZEC two-bar reversal.** [An earlier working paper](ZEC-TWO-BAR-REVERSAL.md) found that ZEC's next 10-minute candle was often down after two up candles. On HYPE, after one or two up 10-minute bars and a first close below the open, price continued down 39% to 53% of the time over 5, 10 and 20 minutes. The unconditional rate was 49.5% to 49.9%. The study has 72 combinations of setup, trigger, horizon and overlap rule, and the confidence interval of 66 of them contains that baseline. The six that do not are two results, each repeated across variants, and both point the other way: 41% of 200 cases and 39% of 131 cases.

**Candle shapes.** The rule chosen on validation (two down 5-minute bars in a falling shape, predict up) was right 69% of 29 times in validation and 48% of 25 times in the final test. It lost money there at every cost level.

**Cycles.** 1,638 spectrum and rolling-fit tests gave a smallest corrected p-value of 1.0. The correction's floor is 0.819: with this many tests, no corrected p-value could fall below it, so the tests could not have detected a cycle. The result is inconclusive, not a proof of absence. The fitted cycle forecast was worse than assuming that price stays where it is.

**Leading correlations.** We tested 18 features at six horizons. None survived the correction on the final test. The largest training correlation, the last minute's BTC return against HYPE's next hour (−0.24), kept its sign but not its significance (p = 0.95).

## 6. Price levels

### 6.1 The level map

Sides are relative to the last hourly close, $65.40. Prices are Hyperliquid perpetual prices. Volume zones spread each bar's volume across its range. The PDF edition charts the map as Figure 2.

| Zone | Side | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| $95.34–98.00 | Resistance | All-time high $98.00 on 2026-09-23; three daily swing highs to 2026-10-29 |
| $75.99–95.65 | Resistance | 70% of the last 90 days' volume traded here; most-traded price $81.10 |
| $74.30–78.35 | Resistance | Twenty hourly swings in four adjoining groups, latest 2026-11-13; four daily swings at $75.15–77.00, including the June highs $75.83 and $77.00. 50-day average $76.13 |
| $71.04–72.91 | Resistance | Six hourly swings, latest 2026-11-16 |
| $68.62–70.25 | Resistance | Eight hourly swings, latest 2026-11-23; the week's high. The 200-day average is just above, at $70.40 |
| $67.76–68.34 | Resistance | Four hourly swings from June and July; the 20-day average is just below, at $67.72 |
| $65.43–66.14 | Resistance, just above | Five hourly swings from June and July |
| $64.50–65.10 | Support, just below | Five hourly swings, latest 2026-11-18 |
| $62.42–63.35 | Support | Four hourly swings from May to July |
| $59.70–60.55 | Support | Five hourly swings and the 2026-11-14 daily low $59.70; a volume node sits just above, at $60.68 |
| $57.96–59.47 | Support | Three daily swings, including the September 2025 high $59.47; seven hourly swings at $57.96–58.55 |
| $55.28–56.50 | Support | Nine hourly swings, latest 2026-11-25; the 2026-11-21 low $55.74 |
| $51.08–54.00 | Support | Five daily swings at $51.08–52.61, including the 2026-08-02 low; eight hourly swings at $52.61–54.00 |
| $49.59–50.16 | Support | Three daily swing highs from 2025, including the July 2025 high $49.89 |
| $42.50–45.84 | Support | Six daily swings; the most-traded price of the two years, $43.63 |
| $38.16–41.71 | Support | Twelve daily swings; volume node $38.69 |

Zones merge adjacent swing groups, so a zone can be wider than the grouping limit in section 3. The table lists selected zones; the price-structure report in section 10 lists every level. Over the full two years, 70% of volume traded between $18.01 and $54.63. Over the last 90 days, 70% traded between $75.99 and $95.65. Most recent volume therefore traded above the price at the time of the study.

### 6.2 Did the levels work?

Each test is a return to a swing level that was already confirmed and not yet broken, entered at that bar's close. Tests on one side do not overlap. A level held when no close in the horizon went through it by the touch tolerance (1.5% daily, 0.5% hourly).

The fair comparison is not the average bar, because every test follows a move toward the level. The placebo columns apply the same rules to lines 6% (daily) or 2% (hourly) above and below each swing level. If swing levels mattered, they would hold more often than those lines.

| Bars and horizon | Side | Tests | Held | Average after | Standard error | Placebo tests | Placebo held | Placebo average after |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Daily, 5 days | Support | 31 | 48% | +1.09% | 1.90% | 43 | 42% | +1.19% |
| Daily, 5 days | Resistance | 30 | 37% | +3.82% | 1.95% | 49 | 39% | +1.98% |
| Daily, 10 days | Support | 23 | 35% | +3.06% | 3.83% | 31 | 42% | +4.53% |
| Daily, 10 days | Resistance | 23 | 39% | +5.56% | 3.77% | 32 | 31% | +3.76% |
| Hourly, 24 hours | Support | 46 | 26% | −0.67% | 0.46% | 78 | 35% | −0.31% |
| Hourly, 24 hours | Resistance | 45 | 33% | −0.36% | 0.83% | 65 | 28% | −0.04% |
| Hourly, 72 hours | Support | 29 | 10% | −0.77% | 1.28% | 36 | 14% | −1.13% |
| Hourly, 72 hours | Resistance | 29 | 17% | +0.51% | 1.75% | 37 | 22% | +0.48% |

The average over all bars was +1.81% for 5 days, +3.50% for 10 days, +0.31% for 24 hours and +0.84% for 72 hours.

The swing levels did no better than arbitrary lines nearby. They held between 10% and 48% of the time; the placebo lines held between 14% and 42%. The largest gap between real and placebo, in hold rate or in average return, is about one standard error. A level broke more often than it held on every row.

The levels mark where price turned before. On this history they did not make a return to the level a reliable turn. They are reference prices for where price paused before. The test gives no reason to prefer them to nearby lines, and they are not an entry signal.

## 7. Agreement with other runs

Two other runs of the same question exist, on partly different data. They differ in venue and window but not in method: the strategy runs share one code base and catalogue. A third piece of work is a forward test that has started and has no result yet.

| Question | [Coinbase run](results/hype_suite_20261127.md) | [31-day Binance run](results/hype_study_2026-11-27.md) | This paper |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data | Coinbase HYPE/USD: a 46-hour gap-free minute run, and 294 days of 5-minute, hourly and daily bars | Binance HYPE/USDT: 44,640 consecutive minute bars over 31 days; Hyperliquid daily and hourly | Binance HYPE/USDT: 10,080 minute bars over 7 days; Hyperliquid daily and hourly |
| Is any strategy validated? | No. Every validation-selected rule in the 294-day run lost on test; the 46-hour minute run's 5-minute pick was positive on about 9 hours of test bars | No. Most validation-selected picks did not hold | No. Nothing beat holding over two years; no hourly rule made money in both parts |
| Hourly RSI dip buying | RSI 14 (30 → 55) +16.7% on its test window | RSI 14 (30 → 55) +8.2% on its test window | RSI 14 (30 → 50) +12.7% in the falling last 30%, after −3.2% in the rising part |
| Short-horizon patterns | None significant after correction | None: no cycle, no leading correlation, no usable two-bar reversal | Two-bar reversal, shapes and leading correlations fail; cycle tests inconclusive |
| Support and resistance | No edge over a moving-average control | Out of sample, levels held 52.1% of 71 tests, inside a random-level control (mean 53.4%) | No edge over offset placebo lines |

The three agree that no rule, pattern or level has an edge, wherever they overlap. Because they share a code base and the same recent weeks of market history, that is weaker than three independent confirmations, but it shows the negative result does not hinge on one venue's data.

They disagree most clearly in one place, and the disagreement is the most useful thing in the comparison. This paper's week ranks ATR-sized trend following first on 5-minute bars. The 31-day run, which contains this week, reports that the trend-following families it lists (ATR-sized, EMA crossover, Ichimoku, moving-average crossover and SMA regime) lost money over the full window: none of the 5-minute ATR-sized settings was positive, and the family's median was −38%. Its best individual rules over the month were dip buyers and Keltner breakouts. **The ranking flips with the window.** The week's result describes a single week that ended in a rally. It should not be extrapolated.

A 14-day forward trial of the hourly RSI dip buyer (RSI 14, buy below 30, exit above 55) began on 2026-11-27 at 13:00 UTC and ends on 2026-12-11. It uses simulated accounts only. It has no result yet, and fourteen days will hold only a few trades, enough to check a hypothesis but not to tell an edge from noise. The trial uses the exit above 55 that the two other runs tested; this paper's own hourly table used an exit above 50. [A companion paper](results/hype_walk_forward_2026-11-27.md) reports rolling walk-forward tests of that rule and how the trial will be read.

## 8. Limits

- **One week holds few independent market states.** The week's winners were chosen from 1,707 overlapping templates, and the best of many is biased upward.
- **The whole-week returns include the training part.** Only the validation and final-test columns are out of sample, and each covers about 34 hours.
- **Costs are modelled.** Spreads, depth, latency, funding and real fills are absent. The reference accounts have no capacity model.
- **No short side with real funding.** Every registered strategy is long or flat, and the one synthetic long/short model pays a flat carry. Whether shorting the falls would have paid is untested.
- **The long-history tests use default parameters and one split,** with no correction for testing 30 strategies at once.
- **The level tests reuse one history.** The hourly levels come from 208 days that contain one rise and one fall.
- **Perpetual prices stand in for spot** over the two years, because none of the three venues checked has a spot history that long.

Parts of the ZEC suite could not be repeated for HYPE: the 25× five-minute walk-forward on Jupiter (it needs weeks of captured prices and funding for that market), order-book replay, and the long-history studies that need inputs HYPE does not have.

## 9. What would count as evidence

None of the rules above is ready to be traded. A rule would earn more trust under the following protocol.

1. Freeze one rule and its parameters before looking at new data. Record the freeze.
2. Run it forward on closed bars, on paper, for a fixed number of bars decided in advance. Do not stop early because the result looks good.
3. Score it against holding and against cash on the same clock, at two fee levels, and again with fills one bar late.
4. Keep every signal and every abstention. Report the number of trades, the worst decline and the result against holding, not the hit rate alone.
5. Repeat across a rising and a falling period before drawing a conclusion. The hourly result in section 4.3 shows why one period is not enough.
6. Test the short side with a model of real funding before making any claim about it.

Two candidates are worth that test: the 5-minute ATR-sized trend rule, which this week favours and the 31-day run does not, and the hourly RSI dip buyer, which is already running on paper (section 7).

## 10. Reproducibility

The files behind the numbers in this paper are public.

- [The underlying study](HYPE-STUDY.md), with the same tables.
- [The weekly run report](../json/hype-week-20261127/report.md) and [the price-structure report](../json/hype-structure-20261127/structure.md).
- [The weekly run's evidence](https://github.com/mithudso/solmargintrader/tree/master/research/json/hype-week-20261127): the report, a summary, and the complete run as one archive.
- [The long-history evidence](https://github.com/mithudso/solmargintrader/tree/master/research/json/hype-structure-20261127): the venue's raw responses, the candles as CSV, the structure results and six backtest comparisons.
- [The price-structure code](https://github.com/mithudso/solmargintrader/blob/master/research/scripts/coin_structure.py). It accepts any Hyperliquid perpetual with at least 60 daily and 336 hourly bars.

Weekly run archive SHA-256:
```
bee60069b6d72d3a93e1c48ea214d5072306b35eaf326749c0f4823c4d334874
```

Hyperliquid HYPE daily candles, CSV SHA-256:
```
34e989c41c7c4e7cb5bac827fea1457a17d921b6293d01d8703bd8fac3779b4b
```

Hyperliquid HYPE hourly candles, CSV SHA-256:
```
0ed4ae5d1a0af4cb5e837ff643786ce9e4ddd2063ae61d56e8dd659fcb8d4e50
```

To verify the weekly run offline and rebuild the structure report, with Python 3.13 and the requirements in `backtester/requirements.txt`, from the root of a local clone of the repository linked above:

```
python -m zipfile -e research/json/hype-week-20261127/artifacts.zip hype-week-check
python -m research.coin_week --output hype-week-check --phase verify
python -m research.coin_structure analyze --output research/json/hype-structure-20261127
```

To run a fresh week and a fresh history:

```
python -m research.coin_week --coin HYPE --output hype-week-new
python -m research.coin_structure fetch --coin HYPE --output hype-structure-new
python -m research.coin_structure analyze --output hype-structure-new
```

The weekly run was verified offline: 78 artifacts and 491,712 strategy rows matched their recorded hashes and counts. The numbers in this paper were then checked against the stored results by a separate review, which recomputed the tables from the data. The mismatches it found were corrected before publication.

## Conclusion

HYPE rewarded holders over two years and punished them with seven declines of a quarter or more on the way. No tested rule turned that history into a better return than holding, and the rules that looked best on one stretch lost on the next. Over the two years, the one benefit seen for trend rules was a smaller worst decline in exchange for some of the gain. The patterns that traders look for on short charts were not found in this data, and price levels are places where price turned before, not places where it was shown to turn again. The next step is a frozen rule run forward on paper, judged against holding.

hype-study-4441b222.body:
# HYPE: strategies, patterns and price levels

Version: 1.0.1. Data frozen 2026-11-27 08:49–08:53 UTC. HYPE traded near $65.60 on
Binance spot; the last completed Hyperliquid hour closed at $65.40.

This repeats the ZEC candle studies on HYPE and adds a two-year look at price
structure. Every result is a backtest or a description of past candles. None of
it qualifies a live trading edge, and nothing here was traded.

The working-paper edition, with two figures and a comparison against the
31-day Binance run, is [What holds up on HYPE?](HYPE-STRATEGIES-PATTERNS-LEVELS.md).

## Short answers

**Which strategies performed best?** It depends on the bar size and on whether
the market was rising or falling. No rule won at every size, and over two years
nothing beat holding.

| Horizon | Best performer in the test | Result | How far to trust it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Daily, two years | Buy and hold | +389%, with a 68% worst decline | No tested strategy beat it. A 20/50-day moving-average crossover kept +173% with a 40% worst decline. |
| Hourly, 208 days | Bollinger breakout (20 bars, 2 deviations) | +107% against +59% for holding at 6 bps, with a 17% worst decline against 42% | Made all of it in the rising part and lost 1.5% in the falling part. At 25 bps it made +49% and trailed holding. |
| 5 and 10 minutes, one week | ATR-sized trend following | +14% to +16% in a week where holding made +0.3% to +0.5% | Positive in validation and final test, at 10 and at 60 bps per fill. One week only. |
| 1 hour, one week | MACD + PPO + RSI average | +4.6% | Positive in validation and final test. Small. |
| Falling market, hourly | Oversold bounce (RSI under 30 plus lower-band touch) | +26.7% while holding lost 28.6% | Lost 1.2% in the rising part before it. Not robust to regime. |
| 1 minute | Nothing | 68 of 1,707 strategies made money at the lowest fee, 19 at the highest | None passed the validation-and-test screen. |

Every strategy tested is long or flat. No short side was tested.

**Which patterns exist?**

- Large, frequent declines. Seven of 25% or more in two years, two of them
  deeper than 65%.
- No day-to-day memory: daily return autocorrelation is +0.009. Volatility
  clusters mildly (absolute-return autocorrelation +0.116).
- HYPE moves with Bitcoin and moves further: correlation 0.54, beta 1.26 over
  two years; 0.59 and 1.04 over the last 90 days.
- A quarter of all volume trades between 13:00 and 16:59 UTC. The largest hourly
  moves fall at 14:00 and 15:00 UTC.
- Wednesday was the strongest weekday (+1.26% average). It does not survive a
  correction for testing seven days.
- The ZEC two-bar reversal pattern does not transfer. No cycle, no leading
  correlation and no reversal shape survived its own controls.

**Where are support and resistance?** See [the level map](#price-levels). The
nearest zones are $65.43–66.14, $67.76–68.34 and $68.62–70.25 above, and
$64.50–65.10, $62.42–63.35 and $59.70–60.55 below. Past returns to such levels
broke them more often than they held, and they held no more often than
arbitrary lines nearby.

## What was run

| Study | Data | Size |
|---|---|---|
| [Weekly candle study](../json/hype-week-20261127/report.md), the ZEC transfer | Binance spot HYPE/USDT, 10,080 one-minute bars, 2026-11-20 08:49 to 2026-11-27 08:49 UTC, no missing minute | 1,707 strategy templates × 6 filters × 4 bar sizes × 4 fee levels × 3 time splits, plus cash and holding benchmarks: 491,712 rows, 441,888 completed. Plus 7,920 Volty, grid and DCA rows, 1,638 cycle tests, correlation tests of 18 features at six horizons and the reversal studies |
| [All-strategy walk-forward](../json/hype-structure-20261127/backtests/all-1d-spot-6bps/report.md) | Hyperliquid perpetual candles: 722 daily bars from 2024-12-05, 4,999 hourly bars from 2026-05-03 | 34 registered strategies, first 70% against last 30%, at 6 and 25 bps, long or cash, and as a 1× perpetual long with a borrow fee |
| [Price structure](../json/hype-structure-20261127/structure.md) | The same Hyperliquid candles, plus BTC, ETH and SOL daily | Swing levels, volume by price, level tests, calendar effects, declines, co-movement |

Coinbase HYPE/USD was not used here. Its minute candles have gaps: the
[Coinbase HYPE suite](results/hype_suite_20261127.md) found that the longest
gap-free minute run in 31 days was 46 hours. Binance's first HYPE/USDT daily
candle is dated 2026-09-24 (seen at fetch time, not archived), so the long
history comes from Hyperliquid, where HYPE has traded since late 2024. USDT is not USD, and a perpetual is not spot; each
table names its market.

## Strategy results

### One week of minute bars

The week ended where it began: $65.63 to $65.60, between $55.80 and $69.80. The
training part fell 4.9%, the validation part fell 1.5% and the final-test part
rose 6.8%.

Share of the 1,707 unfiltered strategies that made money over the whole week:

| Bar size | At 10 bps per fill | At 60 bps per fill | Holding, 10 bps |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 minute | 4.0% | 1.1% | −0.2% |
| 5 minutes | 44.1% | 4.9% | +0.3% |
| 10 minutes | 65.4% | 10.0% | +0.5% |
| 1 hour (1,027 completed) | 66.4% | 38.7% | +0.6% |

Each fee level also pays a 2 bps execution allowance per fill.

The strictest screen asks for at least ten validation exits and a positive
return in validation, in the final test and over the whole week, at both 10 and
60 bps. Twelve distinct 5-minute policies pass (nine ATR-sized, two GARCH
volatility-target, one volatility-target), three 10-minute policies and three
1-hour policies. No 1-minute policy passes.

| Bars | Policy | Whole week, 10 bps | Whole week, 60 bps | Validation / test, 60 bps | Worst decline | Exits |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 5m | ATR-sized: ATR 45, risk 1%, stop 2 ATR, trend 200 | +16.3% | +4.1% | +2.6% / +3.5% | −6.4% | 76 |
| 5m | ATR-sized: ATR 30, risk 1%, stop 1.5 ATR, trend 200 | +16.5% | +4.0% | +3.6% / +3.5% | −7.4% | 40 |
| 10m | ATR-sized: ATR 30, risk 1%, stop 2 ATR, trend 100 | +14.3% | +4.1% | +1.2% / +0.7% | −4.6% | 98 |
| 1h | Average of MACD 12/26/9, PPO 12/26/9 and RSI 14 (30 → 50) | +4.6% | +0.5% | +1.3% / +0.6% | −5.7% | 40 |

The selection rule frozen before the test (best validation return, ten exits)
picked the 5-minute ATR 30 row. Its final test returned +6.6% at 10 bps
on three exits, while holding returned +6.8%. So the test confirms the rule did
not lose in a rally; it does not show it beats holding in one. Under 3.2% of
strategies beat holding in the final test at any bar size.

Median whole-week return of one-member strategies on 5-minute bars at 10 bps,
grouped by that member's rule. About one in eight also carries a gate or
switch, and each family spans several parameter settings:

| Best families | Median | Worst families | Median |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| ATR-sized trend | +9.9% | PPO | −15.5% |
| Moving-average regime | +9.0% | Dual momentum | −13.3% |
| EMA crossover | +8.4% | MACD | −8.7% |
| Keltner breakout | +8.1% | Z-score reversion | −8.0% |
| Ichimoku | +6.9% | Bollinger reversion, stochastic | −7.3% |

On 5-minute bars this week, slow trend filters with wide stops made money and
fast oscillators and reversion rules lost. That did not hold at other sizes: on
1-minute bars the ATR-sized family's median was −31.5% and no family had a
positive median except DCA.

Other models from the ZEC suite, at 10 bps:

- **Volty breakout stops, synthetic 1× long/short.** On 1-minute bars none of
  150 runs made money. On 5-minute bars 3% did. On 1-hour bars 60% did, and 13
  of 50 settings were positive in validation and in the final test even on the
  least favourable intrabar path. The best of those, length 2 with 1.25 ATR,
  made +28.6% over the week. On 10-minute bars six settings
  passed the same screen; length 4 with 1.25 ATR made +17.9%.
- **Ladder grid.** All eight reference grids made money on 5-minute and 1-hour
  bars (median +2.2% and +2.7%, best +4.2%). The week's range suited a grid.
- **DCA with safety orders.** Ten of twelve were positive on 5-minute bars and
  all twelve on 1-hour bars (median +0.3% and +0.6%, best +4.8%).

### Two years of daily bars

Hyperliquid perpetual candles, 2024-12-05 to 2026-11-26. Long or cash, 6 bps fee
plus 2 bps slippage, signals fill at the next open. The first 70% ends on
2026-04-23.

| Strategy | Total return | Sharpe | Worst decline | Trades | First 70% | Last 30% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Buy and hold | +389.4% | 1.29 | −68.0% | 1 | +224.7% | +51.0% |
| Moving-average crossover 20/50 | +172.7% | 1.09 | −39.7% | 6 | +107.8% | +31.5% |
| Moving-average ribbon 5×10 | +138.4% | 1.03 | −42.2% | 209 | +71.6% | +39.2% |
| Time-series momentum, 60 days | +124.6% | 0.94 | −58.3% | 16 | +77.9% | +26.4% |
| VWAP reversion 20 / 2% | +96.9% | 0.84 | −46.9% | 41 | +51.0% | +30.5% |
| Volatility target 60% | +89.7% | 0.93 | −44.3% | 180 | +54.5% | +22.9% |

Fourteen of 30 distinct strategies made money in both parts (the registry also
lists holding itself and three copies of MACD). None beat holding in either
part. Reversion rules made money here too: Z-score +83.5%, stochastic +76.4%,
against +29.4% for the Bollinger breakout. In a market that rose 389%, any
long-or-flat rule that stays invested much of the time collects part of the
rise. At 25 bps the crossover still returned +166.6% and the ribbon +125.7%.
The crossover's case is risk, not return: it gave up 56% of the gain and took
42% less of the worst decline.

A 1× perpetual long under the backtester's Jupiter-style borrow fee kept +143.4%
of the +389.4%, paid $15,084 in borrow fees on $10,000 and was liquidated once
in the model. That run also set the backtester's short permission, but no
registered strategy emits a short, so it tests the borrow fee and nothing else.

### 208 days of hourly bars

2026-05-03 to 2026-11-27. The first 70% (to 2026-09-25) rose 122%. The last 30%
fell 28.6%.

| Strategy | Total return | Sharpe | Worst decline | Trades | First 70% | Last 30% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Bollinger breakout 20 / 2 | +106.8% | 2.78 | −17.0% | 86 | +110.0% | −1.5% |
| EMA crossover 50/200 | +87.9% | 2.07 | −22.7% | 10 | +91.9% | −1.3% |
| 200-bar average regime | +83.2% | 2.02 | −25.8% | 78 | +104.2% | −10.3% |
| Buy and hold | +58.8% | 1.37 | −42.1% | 1 | +122.4% | −28.6% |
| Oversold bounce (RSI < 30 and lower-band touch) | +25.2% | 2.41 | −8.8% | 60 | −1.2% | +26.7% |
| RSI 14 (30 → 50) | +9.1% | 0.60 | −21.9% | 35 | −3.2% | +12.7% |

No strategy made money in both parts. The trend rules beat holding because they
stood aside for most of the fall. The bounce rules made money only in the fall.
At 25 bps only the EMA crossover (+80.9%) still beat holding (+58.2%), and the
oversold bounce fell to −0.3% overall.

## Patterns

### What the data supports

- **Large, frequent declines.** Seven declines of 25% or more since December
  2024: −73.7% over 107 days, −34.0% over 5, −28.9% over 19, −65.6% over 125,
  −30.6% over 9, −33.7% over 47, and the present one, −43.1% from $98.00 on
  2026-09-23 to $55.74 on 2026-11-21. A decline is counted as finished only when
  price makes a new high, so the six finished ones say nothing about how the
  present one ends.
- **High volatility.** 102% annualized over two years, 83% over the last 30
  days. The 14-day average true range is 9.7% of price.
- **Bitcoin beta above one.** Daily correlation with BTC 0.54, beta 1.26. With
  ETH 0.56 and 0.83, with SOL 0.56 and 0.74. Over the week of minute bars the
  same-minute correlation with BTC was 0.73.
- **A US-hours volume peak.** 13:00–16:59 UTC carries 26.4% of hourly volume.
  Average absolute hourly moves peak at 0.82–0.83% at 14:00 and 15:00 UTC and
  bottom at 0.49–0.50% at 06:00 and 09:00 UTC.
- **Swings of 1% a few hours apart.** In the week of minute bars, 1% peaks came
  a median 145 minutes apart and dips 158 minutes apart. The spacing was more
  even than 95% of shuffled paths in 5 of 24 comparisons, uncorrected. The
  formal cycle tests below found no clock to trade on.

### What the data does not support

- **Weekday effects.** Wednesday +1.26% (t = 2.18, 103 days), Tuesday −0.31%,
  Thursday −0.42%. Seven tests need |t| near 2.7. None reaches it.
- **Hour-of-day direction.** 01:00 UTC averaged −0.13% (t = −2.17). Twenty-four
  tests need |t| above 3. None reaches it.
- **Buying big down days.** After a daily loss of 10% or more the next day
  averaged +2.30% (standard error 1.26%, 18 cases). After a gain of 10% or more
  it averaged +1.86% (35 cases). The average day returned +0.35%. Neither case
  separates from the other, and each is within two standard errors of the
  average day.
- **The ZEC two-bar reversal.** After one or two up ten-minute bars and a first
  close below the open, price continued down 39% to 53% of the time over 5, 10
  and 20 minutes. The unconditional rate was 49.5% to 49.9%. Of 72 intervals,
  66 contain the baseline. The six that do not are two results, each repeated
  across variants, and both point the other way: 41% of 200 cases (one up bar,
  intrabar trigger, 5 minutes) and 39% of 131 cases (two up bars, midpoint
  trigger, 20 minutes, non-overlapping).
- **Reversal shapes.** The rule chosen on validation (two down 5-minute bars in
  a falling shape, predict up) was right 69% of 29 times in validation and 48%
  of 25 times in the final test, and lost money there at every cost level.
- **Cycles.** 1,638 spectrum and rolling-fit tests, smallest corrected p-value
  1.0. The correction's floor of 0.819 makes this inconclusive, not a proof of
  absence. The fitted cycle forecast was worse than assuming price stays put.
- **Leading correlations.** 18 features at six horizons. None survived the
  correction on the final test. The largest training correlation, the last
  minute's BTC return against HYPE's next hour (−0.24), kept its sign but not
  its significance (p = 0.95).

## Price levels

Levels are swing highs and lows that were the extreme of 5 days each side (daily)
or 24 hours each side (hourly). Swings are grouped so that no group is wider
than 3% (daily) or 1.2% (hourly). Volume zones spread each bar's volume across
its range. Prices are Hyperliquid perpetual prices, which can differ slightly
from Binance spot. Sides are relative to the last hourly close, $65.40.

| Zone | Side | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| $95.34–98.00 | Resistance | All-time high $98.00 on 2026-09-23; three daily swing highs to 2026-10-29 |
| $75.99–95.65 | Resistance | 70% of the last 90 days' volume traded here; most-traded price $81.10 |
| $74.30–78.35 | Resistance | Twenty hourly swings in four adjoining groups, latest 2026-11-13; four daily swings at $75.15–77.00, including the June highs $75.83 and $77.00. 50-day average $76.13 |
| $71.04–72.91 | Resistance | Six hourly swings, latest 2026-11-16 |
| $68.62–70.25 | Resistance | Eight hourly swings, latest 2026-11-23; the week's high ($69.70 on Hyperliquid, $69.80 on Binance). 200-day average $70.40 |
| $67.76–68.34 | Resistance | Four hourly swings from June and July; 20-day average $67.72 |
| $65.43–66.14 | Resistance, just above | Five hourly swings from June and July |
| $64.50–65.10 | Support, just below | Five hourly swings, latest 2026-11-18 |
| $62.42–63.35 | Support | Four hourly swings from May to July |
| $59.70–60.55 | Support | Five hourly swings and the 2026-11-14 daily low $59.70; volume node $60.68 |
| $57.96–59.47 | Support | Three daily swings, including the September 2025 high $59.47; seven hourly swings at $57.96–58.55 |
| $55.28–56.50 | Support | Nine hourly swings, latest 2026-11-25; the 2026-11-21 low $55.74 |
| $51.08–54.00 | Support | Five daily swings at $51.08–52.61, including the 2026-08-02 low; eight hourly swings at $52.61–54.00 |
| $49.59–50.16 | Support | Three daily swing highs from 2025, including the July 2025 high $49.89 |
| $42.50–45.84 | Support | Six daily swings; the most-traded price of the two years, $43.63 |
| $38.16–41.71 | Support | Twelve daily swings; volume node $38.69 |

### Did the levels work?

Each test is a return to a swing level that was already confirmed and not yet
broken, entered at that bar's close. Tests on one side do not overlap. A level
held when no close in the horizon went through it by the touch tolerance (1.5%
daily, 0.5% hourly).

The fair comparison is not the average bar, because every test follows a move
toward the level. The placebo columns apply the same rules to lines 6% (daily)
or 2% (hourly) above and below each swing level. If swing levels mattered, they
would hold more often than those lines.

| Bars and horizon | Side | Tests | Held | Average after | Standard error | Placebo tests | Placebo held | Placebo average after |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Daily, 5 days | Support | 31 | 48% | +1.09% | 1.90% | 43 | 42% | +1.19% |
| Daily, 5 days | Resistance | 30 | 37% | +3.82% | 1.95% | 49 | 39% | +1.98% |
| Daily, 10 days | Support | 23 | 35% | +3.06% | 3.83% | 31 | 42% | +4.53% |
| Daily, 10 days | Resistance | 23 | 39% | +5.56% | 3.77% | 32 | 31% | +3.76% |
| Hourly, 24 hours | Support | 46 | 26% | −0.67% | 0.46% | 78 | 35% | −0.31% |
| Hourly, 24 hours | Resistance | 45 | 33% | −0.36% | 0.83% | 65 | 28% | −0.04% |
| Hourly, 72 hours | Support | 29 | 10% | −0.77% | 1.28% | 36 | 14% | −1.13% |
| Hourly, 72 hours | Resistance | 29 | 17% | +0.51% | 1.75% | 37 | 22% | +0.48% |

The average over all bars was +1.81% for 5 days, +3.50% for 10 days, +0.31% for
24 hours and +0.84% for 72 hours.

The swing levels did no better than arbitrary lines nearby. They held between
10% and 48% of the time; the placebo lines held between 14% and 42%, and the
largest real-against-placebo gap, in hold rate or in average return, is about
one standard error. The levels mark where price turned before. On this history
they did not make a return a reliable turn, and a level broke more often than
it held on every row.

## How this relates to the Coinbase HYPE suite

A second run of the same request, [the Coinbase HYPE suite](results/hype_suite_20261127.md),
used Coinbase HYPE-USD: 31 days of minute bars cut to a 46-hour gap-free run,
and 294 days of 5-minute, hourly and daily bars from the 2026-02-05 listing. It
named Hyperliquid candles as an unchecked second source. This study is that
check, on a gap-free Binance week and on Hyperliquid's two years.

| Question | Coinbase suite | This study |
|---|---|---|
| Is any strategy validated? | No. Every validation-selected policy lost on test | No. Nothing beat holding over two years, and no hourly rule made money in both parts |
| Hourly RSI bounce | RSI 14 (30 → 55) +16.7% on test, too few validation exits to select | RSI 14 (30 → 50) +12.7% and the oversold-bounce rule +26.7% in the falling last 30%; both lost in the rising part |
| Short test window | 5m positive at all fees on about 9 hours of test bars | 5m ATR-sized positive at 10 and 60 bps on about 34 hours of test bars |
| Short-horizon patterns | None significant on HYPE after correction | Two-bar reversal, shapes, cycles and leading correlations all fail |
| Support and resistance | No edge over a moving-average control | No edge over offset placebo lines |

The two agree where they overlap. The new evidence here is the full week of
minute bars, the 2024–2026 history that the Coinbase listing cannot reach, and
the level map.

## Not transferred from the ZEC suite

- The Jupiter GUM 25× five-minute walk-forward. It needs weeks of captured GUM
  prices and funding for HYPE. The repository's Perps records put HYPE's cap
  there at 25×.
- Order-book replay, the Oracle second-turn, barrier and exit-50 studies, the
  top-50 universe, daily CPCV and the long-history shape router. The weekly
  run's `coverage.json` lists each exclusion and its reason.

## Limits

- One week holds few independent market states. The week's winners were chosen
  from 1,707 overlapping templates; the best of many is biased upward.
- The whole-week returns include the training part. Only the validation and
  final-test columns are out of sample, and each covers about 34 hours.
- Costs are modelled. Spreads, depth, latency, funding and real fills are absent.
  Reference accounts of 10,000 USDT have no capacity model.
- The daily and hourly strategies use default parameters, one split and no
  correction for testing 34 of them.
- The level tests reuse one history. Hourly levels come from 208 days that
  contain one rise and one fall.

## Reproduce

Python 3.13 with `backtester/requirements.txt`, from the repository root.

```bash
cd [local artifact not published]
python -m zipfile -e research/json/hype-week-20261127/artifacts.zip [local artifact not published]
python -m research.coin_week --output [local artifact not published] --phase verify
python -m research.coin_structure analyze --output research/json/hype-structure-20261127
```

A fresh week and fresh history:

```bash
python -m research.coin_week --coin HYPE --output [local artifact not published]
python -m research.coin_structure fetch --coin HYPE --output [local artifact not published]
python -m research.coin_structure analyze --output [local artifact not published]
```

`research.coin_structure` works for any coin Hyperliquid lists. The backtests
ran `python -m backtester.cli --asset HYPE --data <csv> --interval 1d|1h --split 0.7`
with every registered strategy named; each run's `run_manifest.json` records its
inputs.

# Leverage economics — which strategies survive high-fee, high-leverage perps

**AS OF 2026-08-05.** Every figure here is generated by `research/scripts/leverage_economics.py`.
No network, no data files — this is closed-form arithmetic over published venue
parameters, so it reproduces exactly.

```bash
python3 research/scripts/leverage_economics.py --self-test   # gate: 7 load-bearing claims
python3 research/scripts/leverage_economics.py               # all tables
python3 research/scripts/leverage_economics.py --markdown    # the tables below, regenerated
```

> **Educational analysis, not advice.** This is a cost model. It says what a trade must
> overcome, never what a trade will earn.

---

## 1. The result that reframes the question

Write P&L on collateral at leverage `L`:

```
pnl%_collateral  = L·move − (fee_rt·L + rate·util·hours·L)
break_even_move  = fee_rt + rate·util·hours          ← L cancels
```

**Leverage is not in the break-even equation.** A 2× and a 250× position need the *same*
price move to break even. Leverage does not make a trade harder to win.

What it changes is two things and only two things: **how close the absorbing barrier
sits**, and **how fast carry consumes collateral**. Both are survival terms, not
profitability terms. Most "high leverage demands a bigger edge" intuition is misplaced —
the cost of leverage is concentrated entirely in the ruin path.

## 2. The four costs, and what each one kills

| Cost | Magnitude | What it kills |
|---|---|---|
| **Round-trip fee** | 12 bps notional (6 each way) | **Frequency** — multiplied by L *and* by trade count |
| **Borrow carry** | ≤0.016%/hr SOL custody (~140% APR); ≤0.003%/hr stable (~23% APR) | **Duration** — never negative, never pays you. Pure theta. |
| **Liquidation** | **100% of remaining collateral** | **Being eventually right** — path-dependent |
| **Liquidation drift** | Carry accrues against collateral | **Fixed stops** — the barrier walks toward you |

The borrow fee is the one most often misread. It is **not** a funding rate: both sides
always pay, it is never negative, and nobody is ever paid to wait. Longs borrow the
volatile custody, shorts the stable one — which is where the asymmetry in §5 comes from.

## 3. Break-even move by holding period

Utilisation 50%. Leverage-independent, per §1.

| Hold | Long (SOL custody) | Short (stable custody) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 h | 0.128% | 0.121% |
| 4 h | 0.152% | 0.126% |
| 1 day | 0.312% | 0.156% |
| 3 days | 0.696% | 0.228% |
| 1 week | 1.464% | 0.372% |
| 1 month | **5.880%** | 1.200% |

**Carry overtakes the round-trip fee at ~15 h for longs, ~80 h for shorts** (7.5 h / 40 h
at full utilisation). That is the hinge. Below it you are in a fee-dominated regime where
trade *count* is the enemy; above it a carry-dominated regime where *time* is. They
reward opposite behaviour, and a strategy that straddles the hinge pays both.

## 4. The number that should govern leverage choice

Time until carry **alone** zeroes the collateral, with the price perfectly flat:

| Leverage | util 50% | util 100% | Adverse move to liquidate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2× | 260.4 d | 130.2 d | 50.00% |
| 5× | 104.2 d | 52.1 d | 20.00% |
| 10× | 52.1 d | 26.0 d | 10.00% |
| 20× | 26.0 d | 13.0 d | 5.00% |
| 50× | 10.4 d | 5.2 d | 2.00% |
| 100× | 5.2 d | 2.6 d | 1.00% |
| 250× | **2.1 d** | **1.0 d** | **0.40%** |

At 250× you are liquidated in about a day by rent, on a flat chart. And a **0.40%**
adverse move — routine intraday noise on SOL — ends the position at a total loss.

These are the *optimistic* readings: they show when collateral reaches zero, before the
liquidation penalty and before price impact.

## 5. Which strategies survive

### Structurally dead at leverage

**Grid and market-making.** Fee cost is `12 bps × L × round-trip count`:

| Round trips | 1× | 5× | 10× | 20× |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 10 | 1% | 6% | 12% | 24% |
| 50 | 6% | 30% | 60% | 120% |
| 100 | 12% | 60% | **120%** | 240% |
| 500 | 60% | 300% | 600% | 1200% |

**100 round trips at 10× costs 120% of collateral in fees alone.** This is not a tuning
problem; no spacing or level count survives it. It also compounds the closed-trade
illusion already measured for grid unlevered — closed P&L stays positive and green while
the account drains, and leverage accelerates the account line without touching the
closed-trade line.

**Mean reversion and averaging down.** The absorbing barrier removes "eventually right,"
and a martingale into a 100%-penalty barrier is the worst available pairing.

**Long-horizon holds at high leverage.** 5.88%/month break-even for longs at 50%
utilisation, before any price impact.

### What the structure actually favours

- **Few trades, short holds** — under the ~15 h hinge, where fees dominate and carry is
  still small.
- **Convex payoff with a hard stop well inside the liquidation price.** Dying at your stop
  is a partial loss; dying at liquidation is a total one. Those are different events, and
  the distance between them is the entire risk budget.
- **Moderate leverage**, because the liquidation price drifts toward you as carry accrues —
  a stop that was safe at entry converges on the barrier while you hold.
- **Shorts are ~5× cheaper to carry** than longs (stable vs volatile custody) — while open
  interest runs **85–90% long**. The crowd is on the expensive side of the fee schedule.

## 6. Concept family, CVS-scored

Rubric `0.25·Rel + 0.25·Use + 0.20·Nov + 0.15·Int + 0.15·Via`, threshold 3.2, hard gates
Via ≤ 1 or Nov = 0. Arithmetic independently verified: 0 mismatches over 8 rows.

| CVS | Decision | Concept | Why |
|---:|---|---|---|
| **5.00** | RESEARCH | `leverage-cost-arithmetic-and-the-viable-region` | The L-cancellation, the fee/carry hinge, time-to-liquidation-from-carry. Nothing in the skill family states any of it. |
| **4.65** | RESEARCH | `why-high-frequency-strategies-die-at-leverage` | Falsifies "run the grid on leverage" arithmetically; the unlevered grid measurement already exists. |
| **4.65** | RESEARCH | `liquidation-as-an-absorbing-barrier` | Liquidation ≠ stop: 100% penalty, path-dependent, ruin under a barrier. |
| 4.10 | RESEARCH | `stop-placement-under-liquidation-drift` | The existing spoke names the drift but not the stop consequence. |
| 4.05 | RESEARCH | `carry-asymmetry-and-the-crowded-side` | ~5× cheaper shorts against 85–90% long OI. |
| 3.80 | RESEARCH | `holding-window-as-the-primary-parameter` | Partly absorbed by the top concept. |
| 3.65 | RESEARCH | `leverage-sizing-and-risk-of-ruin` | `trading-risk-management` owns Kelly; the barrier is the new part. |
| 3.15 | **SKIP** | `event-driven-short-window-directional` | Via 2 — no catalyst dataset, and it drifts into already-covered signal design. |

That 5.00 is the highest CVS scored across all seven exploration rounds in this line of
work; the prior maximum was 4.70.

## 7. The caveat that outranks everything above

**This is cost structure, not edge.** Across 48 out-of-sample months of prior measurement,
every strategy family tested lost to buy-and-hold *unlevered*, and the parameter sweep's
Deflated Sharpe called every winner indistinguishable from best-of-N luck.

Leverage rescales an edge that already exists. It does not create one. Applied to a
negative edge it simply reaches zero faster — and now with an absorbing barrier, so the
*path* decides the outcome rather than the average.

## 8. Honest limits of this model

- Per-custody rates are **Gauntlet's May-2024 recommendation**, not a live read.
  Utilisation moves continuously; these are order-of-magnitude frames, not quotes.
- **Price impact is not modelled** — the per-custody `factor`/`exp`/threshold are on-chain
  and undocumented, so it cannot be computed from public data. It is strictly additive.
- Also unmodelled: keeper request-to-fill drift, priority fees and Jito tips, failed
  transactions, and the liquidation penalty itself.
- Every omission makes the real picture **worse**, never better.
- Venue parameters change. Verify at `docs.jup.ag` before relying on any figure here.

# Leverage tiers: low, medium, high margin on SOL

Simulation only. Reproduce with `python3 -m research.leverage_tiers --asset SOL --interval 1d`
(about 6 seconds). Raw rows: `research/results/leverage_tiers_sol_1d_summary.csv`,
`research/results/leverage_tiers_sol_1d_per_strategy.csv`, `research/json/results/leverage_tiers_sol_1d.json`.

## Conclusion

**High leverage is ruinous. Medium leverage is nearly as bad. Low leverage does not rescue a losing signal.**
Leverage multiplies the existing result and adds carry, so it can only help a signal that already
works out of sample, and on SOL daily bars almost none do.

At 20x, 99.4% of out-of-sample paths contain at least one liquidation, the median path loses 100% of
capital, and 95% of paths end at or below 10% of starting equity. At 5x, 74% of paths are ruined.
At 2x, 21% are.

## Setup

- Series: SOL daily, 1,875 bars (2021-06-17 to 2026-08-04), the sweep's medium-horizon parameters for all 25 registered base strategies.
- Evaluation: CPCV, 8 blocks, 2 test blocks per path, 28 paths per strategy, 514 pooled paths across the 25 strategies (block 0 has no warm-up history and slow strategies lose further blocks, so fewer than 25 x 28). No parameter is fitted, so no purge applies; warm-up comes from the bars before each block (`backtester/core/cpcv.py`).
- Tiers: low 2x, medium 5x, high 20x (configurable with `--tiers a,b,c`), plus a 1x perp as the unlevered reference on the same cost model.
- Costs on every run: 6 bps open and 6 bps close fee, 2 bps slippage, hourly borrow fee on notional (1.6 bps/hr long at 50% utilization), maintenance margin 0.2%, fill at next bar open.
- Liquidation: fill at the liquidation price (or the bar open if the market gapped through it) moved 50 bps against the position, remaining collateral forfeited. The 50 bps is an assumption, not a venue constant.
- Intrabar: every held bar is checked on the 1m bars (last 30 days) or 1h bars (366 covered days) inside it when a layer covers the bar completely, with borrow fees accrued to the moment of the touch. All other bars use the daily low/high, which is never less severe. Covered days: 26 (1m), 366 (1h), of 1,875. In the 366 days where both feeds exist, the daily low was never more than 5 bps below the lowest hourly low, so the two feeds agree.
- Ruin: equity at or below 10% of the starting capital at any point on a path. Paths concatenate per-block returns as the repo's CPCV does, so ruin is per two-block path, not one continuous history.

## Results (out of sample, pooled over strategies and paths)

| Tier | Leverage | Median OOS path Sharpe | Paths with Sharpe > 0 | Liquidations per path | Paths with a liquidation | Median max drawdown | P(ruin) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1x perp | 1x | -0.390 | 36.6% | 0.01 | 1.4% | 54.2% | 1.2% |
| Low | 2x | -0.445 | 35.8% | 0.35 | 22.0% | 81.3% | 21.0% |
| Medium | 5x | -0.487 | 31.9% | 2.34 | 71.8% | 99.5% | 73.7% |
| High | 20x | -1.571 | 8.9% | 7.11 | 99.4% | 100.0% | 95.3% |

Median compounded path return: -27.5% (1x), -62.1% (2x), -98.3% (5x), -100.0% (20x).

## What survives

Strategy-level medians (per-strategy file) show where the damage concentrates:

- Buy and hold: median Sharpe -0.07 at 1x, -0.11 at 2x, -0.88 at 5x, -1.25 at 20x. P(ruin) 18%, 57%, 100%, 100%.
- Only 4 of 25 strategies have a positive median OOS Sharpe at 1x, 5 at 2x, 3 at 5x, and 0 at 20x.
- The single standout is `hurst_switch`: median Sharpe 0.64 (1x), 0.65 (2x), 0.73 (5x) with zero liquidations, then 0.00 at 20x with a median 100% loss and 80% ruin. Treat it as one of 25 tries. Stele KNOW-596 puts the PBO of this strategy set at 0.700, so the in-sample-best selection is anti-informative, and this table picks it after seeing the outcomes.

## Why leverage cannot help here

- Break-even move is independent of leverage (Stele DOC-714, `research/papers/LEVERAGE-ECONOMICS.md`). Leverage changes only the barrier distance and the carry drag on collateral.
- Barrier distance at entry is about 1/L minus 0.8%: roughly 49% at 2x, 19% at 5x, 4.2% at 20x. SOL moves 4% in a normal day.
- Carry alone is 19 bps of notional per day. At 20x that is 3.8% of collateral per day, so a buy-and-hold position at 20x is liquidated by carry within about 26 days even if price is flat. At 1x, carry alone exhausts collateral in about 1.4 years, which is why even the 1x perp shows liquidations.
- The base signals lose money out of sample (Stele KNOW-632: every spec strategy looked excellent in sample and lost out of sample on these 1,875 bars). Leverage compounds a negative expectation faster.

## Limits of this study

- Daily series only. Hourly SOL has two disclosed gaps and the engine refuses gapped cadence; 1h and 1m enter as intrabar layers instead.
- Intrabar layers cover about 20% of days. Elsewhere the check is the daily low/high. That is the honest limit of the cached data; daily and hourly bars hide intrabar liquidations in the flattering direction (Stele KNOW-657), so the 1x to 20x results are, if anything, optimistic for the uncovered 80%.
- Long/flat only. The wrapped strategies never short. Price-impact fees, keeper latency and priority fees are not modelled and each would worsen the numbers.
- Per-path ruin is a property of two-block concatenations of fresh-capital runs, not a single compounding history.

## Tests

`backtester/tests/test_intrabar_liquidation.py` fails if a liquidation hidden inside a daily bar is missed (hourly wick under a clean daily bar; daily low deeper than the hourly feed; close recovering after a wick), checks the adverse fill and forfeiture, the no-op case when nothing liquidates, the fallback count for uncovered bars, and a no-leak check that the tier decision ignores future bars.

# Trading research synthesis and prospective investment plan

Version: 1.2.0. Evidence cutoff: 2026-11-11. Status: retrospective follow-ups, tiny live validation and installed paper-cohort acceptance complete; future economic evidence remains unqualified. /dr semantic review passed; skill publication is withheld by the owning hub structural gate.

## Decision

Keep new autonomous strategy capital in cash while the frozen paper
comparison runs. The candidate to challenge is unlevered hourly ZEC Bollinger-band
(BB) breakout, with a 40-bar window and bands at 2.5 standard deviations. Compare
it with cash, passive ZEC, a training-volatility-scaled initial ZEC/cash holding
and a fixed BTC/ETH passive allocation. This is a test candidate, not a validated
investment recommendation.

At the actual taker fee, the examined-history replay returns +4.53% for BB,
+129.64% for passive ZEC and +62.14% for the training-scaled ZEC/cash control.
The scaled control also has a smaller maximum drawdown than BB. The replay
window and costs are specified in the follow-up results below. These reused
dates cannot establish a future winner. The evidence does not identify a
strategy that maximizes future profit.

The authenticated Coinbase API observation on 2026-11-11 at 17:07:59 UTC shows
50 bps maker and 90 bps taker commission per side. One basis point (bp) is 0.01%;
these rates are 0.50% and 0.90% on each buy or sell, before execution drag.
The fee observation is retained in
[[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]).
Coinbase One does not establish an API fee waiver. Maker-rate simulations require
separate fill, queue and adverse-selection evidence. The primary prospective
scenario uses the taker rate plus adverse execution costs.

This recommendation concerns new strategy capital. It does not direct a sale of
the owner's existing holdings or modify another strategy's accounts.

## One consolidated evidence file

The current complete machine-readable consolidation is:

[[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published])

Its exact source inventory is:

[[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published])

The file retains 171 distinct source artifacts: the original 146 family artifacts
and 25 additional follow-up, operational and methodology artifacts. It includes
22,913 configuration records and 1,652 ensemble configurations, together with
the other studies below. These are source and configuration counts, not
independent-study counts. Original records, SHA256, units, provenance,
diagnostic/report roles, insufficient cells and invalid-source exclusions remain
visible. The companion JSON preserves complete numerical payloads rather than
replacing unfavorable rows with selected headlines.

The preserved 146-artifact baseline reviewed by the original DDO run is
[local artifact not published]
and its sibling inventory. Later receipts do not alter that fixed baseline.

CSV values retain their original strings. A return fraction of 0.25 means 25%;
`return_pct=25` means 25% over its stated period; `monthly_pct=25` means 25% per
month; and 25 bps means 0.25%. They are different quantities. Nonfinite values remain
explicitly tagged. A CPCV median path return is not a continuously investable
portfolio return. No grand average return or random-effects estimate is computed
across these incompatible and dependent experiments.

## Trial-family results

The consolidation supplies exact source hashes and complete underlying payloads.
Returns below retain each study's original period and cost assumptions. No
common-period conversion is applied here, so the returns are not directly
comparable across rows. DD means maximum drawdown;
OOS means out of sample. CPCV is combinatorial purged cross-validation, PBO is
probability of backtest overfitting, and DSR is the deflated Sharpe ratio statistic.
These diagnostics address selection risk; they do not turn reused prices into
independent observations. Long/flat means holding the coin or cash, without a
short position or borrowed capital.

| Family | Available evidence and denominator | Result and qualification | Principal source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial SOL strategy survey | 953 single-split rows | Historical 70/30 splits; some triples selected after inspecting OOS singles. Exploratory. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
| SOL CPCV | 75 single and 1,046 combination summaries | Daily singles PBO 0.70. Paths and selected combinations reuse prices. Historical prose's 1,287 configuration census differs from current 1,121 rows. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]); [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
| Cross-asset transfer | Fixed defaults across SOL/BTC/ETH/DOGE/ZEC | All 10 off-SOL top-five Sharpe deltas negative. Simpler directional mechanisms travel better than the selected SOL leaderboard. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
| Geometry, perturbation and redundancy | 175 geometry rows per window; parameter neighborhoods and signal correlations | Diagnostics of preceding trials, not independent profitable replications. Correlated votes do not create independent information. | `[local artifact not published]`; `[local artifact not published]`; `[local artifact not published]` |
| Nine-coin monthly walk-forward | Historical report; raw directory unavailable | Report says 48/54 beat hold in sample, 4/54 walk-forward, 54/54 decayed; grids trail hold 9/9. Lower evidence tier because the raw ledger cannot be rechecked here. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
| Corrected resting-grid review | Static SOL ladder plus 8 reset blocks | Account return +32.10% versus hold +88.10%; worst reset block -34.92%. Reset blocks are not a continuous recentering policy. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
| Fixed later grid holdout | 94 daily bars; unchanged configuration | Grid +0.83%, hold +21.60%; two round trips and 80 bars above the ladder. Idle capital matters more than fee sensitivity here. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
| Leverage tiers | 25 strategies, 1x/2x/5x/20x, dependent paths | Median path returns -27.5% / -62.1% / -98.3% / -100%, respectively; 20x has liquidation in 99.4% of paths. Perpetual carry is not spot. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
| Trigger discovery | 13,510 daily and 30,720 hourly hypotheses | Zero triggers meet all declared reliability gates. The 600 saved selected rows are not the full hypothesis denominator. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]); [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
| Costed trigger trades | 20 selected trigger/tier cells | Exploratory trades share the trigger-discovery history. Neither relabeling nor a second table creates fresh validation. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
| Ratio rotation | 144 rows: 72 long-only and 72 neutral | Momentum is stronger than reversion; selected long-only momentum still trails matched ZEC holding and fails its DSR threshold. Short/neutral books do not transport directly to Coinbase spot. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
| Minute common-calendar survey | 200 rows; five profitable | Two positive rows are passive; three are selected VWAP-reversion cells. This was a full-sample preliminary search. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
| Compound defaults | 300 configurations across ten coins | All 5x defaults lose essentially all their OOS stake. Directional hit rate does not establish signed gross expectancy or net profit. | [[local artifact not published]]([local artifact not published]) |
